title: Bobby Deol's Son Graduated from NYU With Honors. He Came Back to Mumbai to Become an Actor.
excerpt: Aryaman Deol studied finance in New York and taught himself filmmaking during COVID. His younger brother Dharam wants in too.
body:
Bobby Deol wanted his son to do anything but this. He made Aryaman study finance. Sent him to New York University. Watched him graduate with honors. Figured the boy would settle in America, build a career on Wall Street, and Bobby would visit him on holidays.

Instead, Aryaman came home to become a Bollywood actor. And his younger brother Dharam? Same plan.

"Both my sons want to become heroes," Bobby said on Aap Ki Adalat this week, with the resigned clarity of a man who's been in this industry for three decades. "What can I do? This industry is such that whether you're a doctor, engineer, or from any other profession, somewhere in your heart, you feel that maybe you can become an actor too."

The NYU-to-Mumbai Pipeline

Aryaman Deol's trajectory reads like a screenplay about the Indian diaspora in reverse. Born in 2001 to Bobby and interior designer Tania Deol, he grew up largely outside the spotlight — a deliberate choice by a family that has watched the Deol dynasty navigate Bollywood's highs and lows across three generations.

Bobby sent him to NYU specifically to create an alternative path. Finance. Numbers. Stability. The kind of career that doesn't depend on Friday box office reports. Aryaman excelled academically and completed his degree with honors.

But during the COVID lockdown, something shifted. Stuck at home like everyone else, Aryaman taught himself filmmaking. Not casually — systematically. He learned editing, sound design, dubbing, and post-production workflows on his own. He started training in dance by watching YouTube tutorials. He rebuilt his physique. By the time the world reopened, the finance graduate had quietly transformed himself into someone preparing for a screen debut.

"He's learning now," Bobby said. "He's trying acting and working on himself. He is very talented. During COVID, when everyone was stuck at home, he taught himself filmmaking. He learned how films are edited, how sound effects are added, how dubbing works. He taught himself everything."

The Deol Dynasty Continues

If Aryaman and Dharam do enter Bollywood, they'll be the fourth generation of Deols in Indian cinema. Their grandfather Dharmendra is one of Hindi cinema's most iconic leading men. Their uncle Sunny Deol delivered some of the biggest action hits of the 1990s and 2000s. Bobby himself has experienced every arc the industry offers — from debut heartthrob to career wilderness to a stunning comeback with Animal and his villainous turn in the Telugu blockbuster Kanguva.

That Bobby actively tried to redirect his sons away from the family business makes this moment different from the typical Bollywood dynasty announcement. This wasn't a launch orchestrated by a powerful father. It was a son who chose cinema over finance after getting the education and exposure to make an informed choice.

Bobby's Own Reinvention

The timing of this revelation is fitting. Bobby is in the middle of his most creatively ambitious phase ever. Bandar, directed by Anurag Kashyap and releasing June 5, features him as a wannabe rockstar accused of sexual assault — a role that premiered at TIFF and represents his first collaboration with one of India's most respected auteurs. After that comes Alpha, Yash Raj Films' spy thriller starring Alia Bhatt and Sharvari, where he plays the antagonist.

From Dharmendra's charisma to Sunny's raw power to Bobby's late-career reinvention, the Deol legacy has been defined by a willingness to evolve. Whether Aryaman and Dharam can add their own chapter remains to be seen. But there's something quietly powerful about a kid who went to NYU, learned what the world outside looked like, and decided he belonged in front of a camera anyway.

The family business, it turns out, is hard to quit.
author: Diaspora Desk
